subject: Pathology
summary: Acid‑base disorders are disturbances in blood pH caused by excess acid or loss of base. Clinicians must identify the primary disorder, assess compensation, and treat the underlying cause.

sections.p: Blood pH is tightly regulated (7.35‑7.45). A disorder is diagnosed by arterial blood gas (ABG) showing pH, PaCO₂, and HCO₃⁻ that do not fit normal compensation.
b: pH < 7.35 = acidemia; pH > 7.45 = alkalemia
Primary disorder: the variable that is out of proportion to the others

t.b: What is the primary acid‑base disturbance? – Determines pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻ and whether compensation is appropriate
Is there an anion‑gap metabolic acidosis? – Calculates AG = Na – (Cl + HCO₃); >12 mEq/L suggests unmeasured acids

sections.p: Severity is graded by pH deviation and the presence of organ dysfunction.
b: Mild: pH 7.30‑7.34 or 7.46‑7.49, no shock
Moderate: pH 7.20‑7.29 or 7.50‑7.55, tachypnea, altered mental status
Severe: pH < 7.20 or > 7.55, hypotension, coma

sections.p: Identify the category (respiratory vs metabolic) then narrow to common etiologies, especially those seen in low‑resource settings.
b: Respiratory acidosis – hypoventilation (COPD, opioid overdose, severe asthma)
Respiratory alkalosis – hyperventilation (pain, sepsis, high altitude, malaria fever)
High‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis – diabetic ketoacidosis, sepsis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, toxic ingestions, severe malaria, TB meningitis
Normal‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis – diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, excessive bicarbonate loss (drainage), chronic diarrhoea from cholera
Metabolic alkalosis – vomiting, nasogastric suction, diuretic overuse, antacid abuse, hyperaldosteronism

sections.p: Symptoms reflect pH and the underlying disease.
b: Acidemia: headache, nausea, Kussmaul breathing, lethargy, arrhythmias
Alkalemia: paresthesias, tetany, seizures, shallow rapid breathing

sections.p: Beyond ABG, targeted tests clarify the cause and assess organ impact.
b: Serum lactate – distinguishes lactic acidosis
Blood glucose – screens for DKA
Renal function – evaluates uremic acidosis
Urine ketones – confirms ketoacidosis

t.b: Is lactic acidosis present? – Elevated >2 mmol/L supports tissue hypoxia or sepsis
Is hyperglycaemia driving metabolic acidosis? – >250 mg/dL suggests DKA
Is renal failure contributing? – High values indicate reduced acid excretion
Are ketones present? – Positive dipstick supports ketoacidosis

sections.p: Uncorrected severe disorders can cause rapid deterioration.
b: Severe acidemia (<7.20) → cardiovascular collapse, arrhythmias
Severe alkalemia (>7.55) → seizures, decreased cerebral blood flow
Persistent high anion gap despite treatment → ongoing toxin exposure or sepsis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct the pH if life‑threatening.
b: Ventilatory support for respiratory acidosis (intubation, adjust ventilator settings)
Treat sepsis, DKA, or toxin exposure promptly
IV sodium bicarbonate only for pH < 7.10 or severe hyperkalemia
Potassium replacement when correcting acidosis to avoid hypokalaemia

sections.p: Re‑check ABG after interventions and address chronic risk factors.
b: Daily ABG or venous bicarbonate until stable
Educate patients on medication adherence (e.g., insulin, antiretrovirals)
Vaccinate against infections that precipitate acidosis (influenza, pneumococcus)
Sepsis‑induced hyperventilation vs primary respiratory alkalosis
Renal tubular acidosis vs diarrhoeal loss of bicarbonate
Mixed disorders can mask pH change; always calculate expected compensation
Low albumin lowers the anion gap – adjust AG = AG + (2.5 – albumin g/dL)
Peripheral venous blood gases may underestimate PaCO₂

whenToSeekHelp: Severe acidemia or alkalemia with altered consciousness
Rapidly falling blood pressure or shock

faq.q: Why is the anion gap useful?
faq.a: It separates metabolic acidosis caused by added acids from that caused by bicarbonate loss.

faq.q: Can a patient have both respiratory and metabolic disorders?
faq.a: Yes; mixed disorders are common and identified when compensation does not match the primary disturbance.
Only when pH is <7.10, severe hyperkalaemia, or specific toxin ingestion; otherwise it may worsen intracellular acidosis.

exam: Interpret an ABG showing pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 50 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22 mEq/L – identify the primary disorder and compensation.
Calculate the anion gap for Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 100, HCO₃⁻ 12, albumin 3 g/dL – state the type of metabolic acidosis.
List three common causes of high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis in a low‑resource setting.
